en: Ebegey’s ribs,
Appeared dimly through the haze.
Of the warrior Üytkör,
Pure in marksmanship,
A gift standing for Manas,
With blazing courage in his faith,
No infidel like the moon among the massed battle,
The blow Manas had drawn,
He watched with imposing force,
Appearing to the eye like the magnanimous hero,
Oil flowed from his fingers,
Blood flowed from his nails,
The place he entered without tiring,
The khan who saw Bishkek would know,
He drew it back and released it,
The bullet passed through and struck the chest,
They called him an eagle-soul made into a bullet,
What a lionhearted warrior he was,
They said he fell into bloody hands,
He was accomplished; he was a hero,
They said he lay crawling upon the earth.
From the edge of his ribs,
It was clear the shot passed straight through,
Blood flowed in repeated streams,
When the blood had poured out,
Life left Ebegey.
The bloodied people began to move,
Their tears lasted all day,
Ebegey, a tiger from his sheath,
Who inhabited Ala-Too,
O dear white-capped Kyrgyz people,
Now they did not merely stand and watch,
Maatörö who swept the foothills,
He trampled while watching the ground,
He slipped beside the blue grave mound,
He stirred, his face turning pale,
Blood filled the hollow of his breast.
Ebegey, father of the people,
Had sacrificed himself for the nation,
Üytkör, stained with much blood,
Girded himself like an eagle,
Called the champion among the brave,
When Ozu attacked in an uproar,
Amid the enemy people,
The people did not know the outcome,
Saying his eye watched the many wicked ones,
Saying he himself was gentler than a sheep,
Destroying his five mountains,
Saying the people applied their wisdom,
Falling from the slope,
Look, he overcame the hardship,
Saying it was his own home,
Calling him the discovered shining soul,
Ebegey, the delight of your people,
Speaking of Ebegey’s head,
He cut off and took his head.
Chongteñir, whose fate was harsh,
Your elder khan, Great China,
He went to announce the glad tidings.
After seeing Ebegey’s head,
That warrior Üytkör,
He saw that he was indeed a hero,
He recognized his marksmanship,
They rejoiced greatly and gathered,
At the grave, the cap fell,
He did what no one else could know,
Üytkör, whose path was hardened,
Today he pursued the feud,
Never satisfied in demanding the deed,
Never ceasing to question,
One would not heed another’s words,
Another accepted the other’s words.
His forefather stood among them,
He would not turn his eye toward a single corner.
Ebegei had spoken and remained,
He meant to tell the khan of your blood,
Our hero Soz had been there.
Of this people wrapped in mist,
When you ask after its deepest roots,
At the thorn planted by your kinsmen,
When you took it without leaving my banner,
A thimble mouth and camel eyes,
Deep dark eyes,
If we do not meet, keep speaking,
From the great one of the ages,
Take the woman with twelve eyes,
In the city where they said to meet,
What now remains in his land,
Take the crown of the wrestler,
Go out against him and travel,
Awake beneath the heavy curse,
His thought vanished into grief,
He said to shoot like the moon,
To go to the place red with flesh,
Esen Khan had nothing to say,
There is a plane tree where the sun rises,
A mottled tea-red day,
I have a land where they said to meet,
There is Kenen who will judge it,
Breaking the enemy's back,
Chyng Tengir brought down the splendor,
Take this tribute I wish to give,
Hear the words of those who came,
Hear the words of the massed army,
Look upon the fierce hero Kenen,
They say he goes to hold the meeting,
They say he saw whomever he encountered.
They say Kurman’s life came to rest.
The armored warrior whom Kurman clad,
The pure warriors who pierced the stone,
Calling him a brave man dressed in his mail,
The heroes did not know it.
They met him with their spears,
The full host of dark Kalmyks.
The armored warrior came out to wrestle.
Those who asked, “What is even a fly?”
From the heart of the one possessed,
Those who consumed it in place of food.
They say turmoil descended and he died.
Taking the enemy without pause,
They say he kept inflicting torment.
They say he crushed Karmush.
From the Kalmyk who summoned his courage,
They say he scattered his blood like water.
The armored man wearing Kurman’s coat,
They say he chased and subdued his spirit.
The armored man called Kuramal,
They say he made him writhe and spilled his blood.
A prince emerged from the bull-like host.
In this contest of the mighty,
They say he pressed him down with a grip.
Fire flared, burning from his core.
An enemy arose from within him.
Like a bullet striking the chest,
It burned through him like a root.
It shattered him and became embers in the fire.
They say he scattered the assembled force with his fist.
If he went among the Kyrgyz and showed hatred,
He would make China present its back.
He pursued him like a maral.
His battle cry was “Buгу”; the enemy was a dog.
He seized the hem and laid waste around him.
He had become corrupted and gone astray,
The forty khans now turned back,
A grievous day settled over China,
Together they reached its foundation,
Forgetting the black calamity,
They had become enemies,
Scattering China’s livestock,
Riding toward the Kyrgyz,
Like honey beneath the water,
It was a day of completion,
A thousand words rose from eyes toward the moon,
He made it forbidden,
Like a star of flame in the sky,
It was a day that came from China.
The strongest of extraordinary words,
He was a son among two hundred,
He was poison destined for China,
A soul that never bent before the sword,
To the forty khans, the Manchu and Mongol,
He went about calling them Chinese,
He saw the Chinese were numerous,
Completing the deed and carrying it forward,
Crossing the promontory land,
One crooked man would depart,
You have long known the two,
Taking hold through words,
I shall stand in the people’s cause,
When they sought a remedy,
He descended into their midst like a judge,
For the merit he had requested,
He did not sit still without struggling,
He became a dear khan over China,
He became the head of the hostile force,
He devastated the Kyrgyz people.
These Kyrgyz are beyond the wind’s reach.
They have ruined your undertaking,
And struck your strength from your waist.
They have laid you in your grave.
Brave Orozan, lord of Chokon’s people,
They have undone the people you set in order.
There is no man left; they have grown numerous.
The enemy behind you has become few.
My strength that had girded itself,
My manly guardian, hold firm.
You will come into this world,
To the resounding shield,
You are a keen and deadly marksman.
You were a wrestler and a champion.
You alone were the one I trusted.
Even if the earth fell before you,
The wind could not overtake you in battle.
Come after binding the people’s hands.
Gouge out both their eyes,
Cut out their tongues without dragging them,
And slash them from the nape.
Exact the Kalmyk’s grief by force.
Kick him in the ribs,
Mount him upon the iron,
Drive him on in humiliation,
Shove him away and burn him,
And drive him here before me.
You were a brave man and a champion.
The broad son of the Burut,
The towering Sungai falcon,
The broad one from Kök-Chalkan,
Your champion who rode out to the contest—
Do not make the road of his horse a drove-road,
His neck was vast as Ala-Too.
He appeared like a shield for the people,
He drained the strength of the multitude,
His arm was a block, his heart stone,
His eloquent tongue stirred great tumult,
Taking position like a variegated army,
So many of the white-capped people,
The condition of hero Kenen,
Find his people and hold them.
Passed down from the storytellers,
Asked of countless youths,
With the swift and famed marksman,
Wading through the surging blood,
Caught in distress,
Koyka Bash, who had become Kyrgyz,
The sword passed and severed his spine,
Hero Üytkör kept his eyes open,
He lost his fierce strength,
At the time he left the battle,
It was a mountain he would climb untired,
He was a warrior who advanced without stopping,
His fur-capped eyes blazed,
No one had another youth like him,
My falcon of the mountains,
He would plunge into bloody battle,
Never retreating from it,
He would lie down with his saddlecloth,
His weary eyes could no longer see,
May the shattered spear not strike,
Kenen watched and was delayed,
Like an unyielding warrior,
He descended without abandoning his stance,
Köböy swayed among them all,
May the living Kyrgyz not abandon him,
Such was the warrior’s lionheartedness.
All that has come down from the forefathers,
He knew with stern attention.
That dark Kyrgyz still rides on.
Upon Beijing’s golden throne,
Where its people were established in splendor,
Saying China would suffer calamity from the Burut,
Saying any man who grappled with him would die.
From the Kyrgyz farther beyond,
It was inscribed under a vanished rule.
Saying, “I shall take the Burut,”
When they heard this news,
The khans rode out from Kaken.
